reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Characterised by giant, cerebriform rugal folds in the gastric body and fundus that typically spare the antrum
Foveolar (mucous cell) hyperplasia with cystic dilatation of glands and loss of parietal cells produces a thickened, boggy mucosa and excess mucus secretion
A protein-losing gastropathy causes hypoalbuminaemia, which may present with peripheral oedema and anasarca
Acid output is characteristically reduced (hypochlorhydria or achlorhydria) because of parietal cell loss
Overexpression of transforming growth factor-alpha (TGF-alpha) with excessive epidermal growth factor receptor signalling is implicated in the adult form
In children the disorder is frequently self-limiting and associated with cytomegalovirus infection

Management is largely supportive, with a high-protein diet and protein replacement; anti-epidermal growth factor receptor antibody therapy has been used in refractory adult disease and gastrectomy is reserved for severe or premalignant cases
The adult form carries an increased long-term risk of gastric adenocarcinoma, so surveillance is prudent
reference.pathophysiology: Menetrier disease is a rare hyperplastic gastropathy in which marked expansion of surface mucous (foveolar) cells with cystic gland dilatation and progressive loss of acid-secreting parietal cells thickens the gastric body and fundus into giant folds. Excessive epidermal growth factor receptor activation, driven by overexpression of transforming growth factor-alpha, is thought to underlie the mucous cell hyperplasia and to suppress acid secretion in the adult form, whereas the paediatric form is often triggered by cytomegalovirus. The abnormal mucosa is leaky, allowing plasma proteins to escape into the gastric lumen, which produces a protein-losing gastropathy with hypoalbuminaemia and dependent oedema.
additionalDifferentials: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with hypertrophic gastric folds
Gastric lymphoma including mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma
Gastric involvement by sarcoidosis or eosinophilic gastritis
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrating enlarged folds, with deep (well or jumbo) biopsies to sample the full mucosal thickness
Serum albumin and total protein to document the protein-losing state
Cross-sectional imaging to assess fold thickness and help exclude malignancy
Gastric acid studies typically showing hypochlorhydria
Testing for cytomegalovirus, particularly in children
Stool alpha-1 antitrypsin clearance to confirm gastrointestinal protein loss
Fasting serum gastrin to exclude a gastrinoma
redFlags: Progressive weight loss, anaemia, or a focal mass raising concern for underlying malignancy
Severe hypoalbuminaemia with anasarca and effusions
Biopsy or imaging features overlapping with infiltrative carcinoma or lymphoma
reference.prognosis: The adult form is usually chronic and may be complicated by disabling protein loss and an elevated risk of gastric adenocarcinoma, whereas the childhood form associated with cytomegalovirus is typically self-limiting and resolves over weeks to months.
pitfalls: Taking superficial biopsies that miss the diagnosis because the characteristic changes lie deep within the mucosa
Attributing hypoalbuminaemia to hepatic or renal disease and overlooking a protein-losing gastropathy
Failing to distinguish giant folds from malignant infiltration or a gastrinoma
Neglecting surveillance for gastric cancer in long-standing adult disease
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Targeted anti-epidermal growth factor receptor therapy with the monoclonal antibody cetuximab in symptomatic adult disease to reduce foveolar hyperplasia and protein loss
High-protein diet with intravenous albumin replacement as needed to counter the protein-losing gastropathy and dependent oedema
Symptomatic acid suppression, anticholinergics or octreotide to lessen mucus and protein losses
Eradication of Helicobacter pylori where detected, and antiviral consideration for cytomegalovirus-associated childhood disease, which is often self-limiting
Endoscopic surveillance with deep biopsies for the recognised risk of gastric adenocarcinoma
Total or partial gastrectomy reserved for intractable protein loss, uncontrollable symptoms or malignant transformation
Gastroenterology-led multidisciplinary follow-up with monitoring of serum albumin and nutritional status
